| Convolutional Neural Network Model based Students’ Engagement Detection in Imbalanced DAiSEE Dataset [https://www.academia.edu/download/105273927/Paper\_71-Convolutional\_Neural\_Network\_Model.pdf](https://www.academia.edu/download/105273927/Paper_71-Convolutional_Neural_Network_Model.pdf) Mayanda Mega Santoni, T. Basaruddin, Kasiyah Junus Abstract Tries to address the issue of data imbalance found in the DAiSEE dataset Imbalance can cause errors in classification model (overfitting, underfitting) Convolutional Neural Network was used for feature extraction on DAiSEE dataset. OpenFace was used for: Facial Landmark detection FAU recognition Eye gaze estimation Head pose estimation Pre processing included Data selection Dimensional reduction PCA & SVD Normalization Later oversampled using SMOTE 80:20 train test split. Achieved a best accuracy of 77.97% using the SVD dimensional reduction technique Introduction Mentions the different types of engagement (behavioral, emotional, cognitive) Emotional engagement is particularly important in education because it has a significant impact on their learning rate and overall academic performance \[2\] CNN is a powerful deep learning model that has been successfully used in various studies to detect students’ engagement levels in online learning. Benchmark accuracy value of DAiSEE dataset for engagement detection was 51.07% \[9\] Imbalance: 1% very low, 5% low, 50% high, 45% very high (engagement) SMOTE boosted by Edited Nearest Neighbours (ENN) method allows for an improvement in classification precision \[13\] To address imbalance: Perform data balancing and feature selection Methodology  Dataset Used DAiSEE Focused solely on engagement levels Feature Extraction Used OpenFace library Facial Landmarks, FAUs, Head Pose, Eye Gaze Data Pre-Processing Data Selection Feature Dimensional Reduction Data Normalization Outcomes of this stage were feature matrices that could be utilized in next stage Imbalanced Dataset Handling Undersampling Oversampling Data Splitting The feature matrix with balanced data was used in training and testing 80:20 Classification Model Input Data: The video recording data collected in feature extraction CNN Classification Model Output: prediction class or engagement level of input data ![][image1] Classification Model Evaluation Evaluated on Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 score Results Dataset Data was highly imbalanced between engagement levels. Low \= 0.7%, Very Low \= 5.1% ![][image2] Feature Extraction Facial features were extracted from each frame. 10 sec \* 30 fps \= 300 frames per video 709 facial feature values (landmark, faus, gaze, head pose) Data Pre-Processing Data Selection Performed group undersampling until it reached the minority threshold (61 which is the total value of the minority class) ![][image3] Dimensional Reduction Each frame had a feature vector of 709, it became necessary to reduce the dimensions of the features to obtain unique features that could be used as differentiators for each level of engagement. Principal Component Analysis Singular Value Decomposition Using PCA and SVD, the number of features was reduced to 300 ![][image4] Normalization Min-Max normalization was applied to produce new feature values ranging from 0 to 1 Imbalanced Dataset Handling SMOTE was used for more balancing after the group undersampling ![][image5] Data Splitting 80:20 training testing split Classification Model Consisted of two stages Feature Extraction Four convolutional and pooling layer combinations Kernel size of 5 with ReLU activation function Classification Max-pooling with a pooling size of 2x2 ![][image6] ![][image7] Conclusion Best PCA-CNN Accuracy: 72.88% F1: 0.73 Best SVD-CNN (Best Overall) Accuracy: 77.97% F1: 0.78 Future directions/recommendations Determine optimal component values Conduct more in-depth analysis of features beyond facial expressions (body pose?) Convolutional Neural Network [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGwBXDKFk9I\&t=134s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HGwBXDKFk9I&t=134s)  Classification of large and complicated images is usually done using something called a CNN. Reduces number of input nodes Tolerate small shifts in where the pixels are in the image Take advantage of the correlations that we observe in complex images Applies a filter to the input image (aka kernel) A smaller square that is commonly 3x3 pixels Intensity of each pixel in the filter is determined by backpropagation Before training a CNN, we start with random pixel values for filter After training with backprop, we end up with something more useful Compute dot product of input and filter To apply filter, overlay filter onto input image and multiply each overlapping pixel, then add each product together \[Dot Product\] By computing the dot product, we can say that the Filter is convolved with the input. Add a Bias term to the output of the filter Put the final value into a Feature Map Slide filter over n pixels (depends) Repeat until feature map is filled Each cell in the Feature Map corresponds to a group of neighboring pixels. Helps take advantage of any correlations there might be in the image. Typically, we run the Feature Map through a ReLU Activation Function All negative values are set to 0, positive values are same as before Apply new filter to feature map Unlike before, we simply select the maximum value. Moves in a way that it does not overlap itself When we select the maximum value in each region, we are applying Max Pooling Alternatively, we could calc the average value for each region and that would be called Average or Mean Pooling. Convert pooled layer into a column of input nodes. Plug input nodes into a normal neural network. NOTE: if we wanted to, we can make the output easier to interpret by running it through a SoftMax function or an ArgMax function. Randomly oversampling the minority class in the training set Cross validation ![][image8] |

| Engagement Detection through Facial Emotional Recognition Using a Shallow  Residual Convolutional Neural Networks  [https://iris.uniroma1.it/retrieve/1eaaa422-7f02-4bb5-8558-8b29885e639e/Iacobelli\_A%20Machine\_2023.pdf](https://iris.uniroma1.it/retrieve/1eaaa422-7f02-4bb5-8558-8b29885e639e/Iacobelli_A%20Machine_2023.pdf)  Michael Moses Thiruthuvanathan,  Balachandran Krishnan, Madhavi Rangaswamy  Abstract Paper proposes creating a CNN and enabling it with residual connections that can  Residual learning carries additional learning from previous batch of layers into the next batch enhance learning rate of the network and improve classification on 3 Indian datasets	 ISED & iSAFE data: 91.3% accuracy DAiSEE data: 93.4% accuracy Introduction CNNs and Residual Networks (ResNet) are considerably used to improve outcomes in emotion detection. Residual Networks utilize skip networks that can connect between layers to enhance the learning pattern of the network. Datasets ![][image9] The Residual Network Uses ResNet for feature extraction from faces ![][image10] Left: Convolutional Layers Right: Skip network Middle: Connection between residual connections and convolutional layers. Experimentation & Results & Discussion 508 images from ISED and iSAFE (7 classes) 5295 images from DAiSEE  ![][image11]  ![][image12] Look into \[28\] and \[29\] (accuracies of 90.89 and 86  Residual Networks [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o\_3mboe1jYI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o_3mboe1jYI)  [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpGugh8NX3U](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpGugh8NX3U)  Classic CNNs have a series of sequential connections between convolutional blocks This sequential connection is quite limiting So the most successful models before ResNet had sequential connections of just 16 and 30 layers. As shown below, as the classic CNN got deeper from 20 layers to 56\. Training becomes extremely challenging ![][image13] Solution: Residual networks Identity/Skip/Shortcut connections Bypass one or more layers ![][image14]  ![][image15] Performance is now better as the number of layer increases The ResNet Block  |
